title: Sorting and counting: like with like, then count each group

summary.text: Tip out a heap of mixed things and ask: which kind is there most of? You cannot tell by looking. You will sort the heap into groups, count each group, and make one mark for each thing. Then you will sort the same heap by a different rule and see what changes and what stays the same. You will also find out that the groups come from the rule you choose.
summary.art: A girl kneeling on a floor beside a heap of clothes clips, crayons and bottle lids, sliding them into three groups on three sheets of paper.

intro.hook: Which are there more of, circles or squares? Look first. Then find a way to check.
intro.text: There are 6 squares and 5 circles. In a jumble it is hard to see. Put the squares together and the circles together, and it becomes easy to count each group. That is sorting. Now look at the colours. There are 7 blue shapes and 4 red shapes. They are the same shapes, sorted in a new way. In this lesson you sort real things from your home, count each group, and see what a new sorting rule does.
intro.art: A jumble of red and blue paper circles and squares on a floor, with a child's hand reaching for one.

outcomes: I can sort things into groups and say the rule I used.
I can count each group and say which has the most and which has the fewest.
I can sort the same things again in a different way.
I can show that sorting does not change how many things there are in all.
I can make one mark for each thing, and count the marks.
I can say that the groups depend on the rule we choose.

terms.meaning: To put things that are alike together.
terms.example: You put all the spoons in one place and all the tumblers in another.
terms.art: Spoons in one group and steel tumblers in another on a kitchen counter.

terms.meaning: Things that have been put together because they are alike in one way.
terms.example: All the red crayons make one group.
terms.art: Five red crayons lying together, apart from a few blue ones.

terms.meaning: The one thing you look at when you sort, such as colour, kind or size.
terms.example: If your rule is colour, a red clip and a red lid go together.
terms.art: A red clothes clip and a red bottle lid side by side, with a blue clip set apart.

terms.meaning: The same in one way. Two things can be alike in one way and different in another.
terms.example: A banana and a lemon are alike in colour. They are different in shape.
terms.art: A banana and a lemon next to each other, both yellow.

terms.meaning: The biggest number. The group with the most has more things than every other group.
terms.example: 6 clips, 5 crayons and 4 lids. Clips have the most.
terms.art: Three rows of things, with the longest row circled.

terms.meaning: The smallest number. The group with the fewest has less than every other group.
terms.example: 6 clips, 5 crayons and 4 lids. Lids have the fewest.
terms.art: Three rows of things, with the shortest row circled.

terms.example: 6 clips, 5 crayons and 4 lids make 15 things in all.
terms.art: Three small groups with one big loop drawn around all of them, labelled 15.

terms.meaning: A short line you draw to stand for one thing. You draw one mark for each thing.
terms.example: Three autos go by. You draw | | | on your paper.
terms.art: A child's paper with three short pencil lines next to a small drawing of an auto.

terms.meaning: Boxes drawn in rows, where you write each group and how many it has.
terms.example: One row says 'spoons' with 6 marks. The next row says 'cups' with 4 marks.
terms.art: A hand-drawn table with two rows, a spoon and a cup drawn at the left, and pencil marks beside each.

explanations.context: This card says what sorting is. You did it in the Heap Test, when you put the things from one heap into groups.
explanations.definition: To sort is to put things that are alike together. The way they are alike is your sorting rule.
explanations.description: A mixed heap is hard to use. First you choose a rule, such as shape. Then you look at each thing and ask which group it belongs to. Here is a worked example. The rule is shape. You pick up a red circle. It is a circle, so it goes with the circles. Its colour does not matter for this rule.
examples: In the kitchen, spoons go with spoons and tumblers go with tumblers.
After the wash, each person's clothes go in that person's pile.
A vegetable seller keeps tomatoes in one heap and onions in another.

perspectives.explanation: In the 1700s Linnaeus sorted plants and animals into groups by features he could see. His method is still the base of how living things are named.
Scientists who study how traditional peoples name nature find that many sort plants by use, place or smell: what heals, what feeds, what grows by water. Each sorting rule is right for its purpose.

explanations.art: A jumble of circles and squares on the left, and on the right the same shapes in two neat groups.

chart.title: The opening puzzle, sorted by shape

explanations.concept: Count each group: most and fewest
explanations.context: This card shows what to do after sorting: count each group and compare. You did this in the Heap Test.
explanations.definition: After sorting, count each group. The biggest number is the most. The smallest number is the fewest.
explanations.description: Look at the picture. There are 6 spoons, 4 cups and 5 lids. Spoons have the most and cups have the fewest. You can also see it without counting. Put each group in a row, one thing in each floor tile. The longest row has the most. Two spoons stick out past the cups. So there are 2 more spoons than cups.
examples: 3 idlis and 5 vadas on a plate. There are more vadas.
In a family of 4 with 3 fans at home, there are more people than fans.
Rows only work if the things are spaced the same. One thing in each floor tile is a good way.

perspectives.explanation: A count of each group is called a frequency. It shows how a whole set is spread out. 'Most' always depends on the rule that made the groups.
Many animals, such as fish and bees, pick the bigger group of food or friends without using number words. So noticing 'more' is older than counting with numbers.

explanations.art: Three rows of kitchen things laid on floor tiles, one thing in each tile: six spoons, four cups and five lids.

explanations.concept: One heap can be sorted in many ways
explanations.context: In the Heap Test you sorted the same things by kind, then by colour, then by your own rule. This card says what you found.
explanations.definition: The same things can be sorted by different rules. Each rule gives different groups.
explanations.description: Take the shapes from the opening puzzle. Sort them by shape and you get circles and squares. Sort the same shapes by colour and you get red ones and blue ones. Both sorts are right. Each one answers a different question. 'How many circles?' needs the shape sort. 'How many red ones?' needs the colour sort. So before you sort, ask what you want to find out.
examples: Clothes can be sorted by whose they are, or by shirts, shorts and towels.
Books can be sorted by size, or by what they are about.
Children in a class can be sorted by age, by height, or by the first letter of their names.

perspectives.explanation: Sorts by use: leaves for the pot, flowers for the altar, roots for the medicine. The same plants are put together in different ways for different jobs.
Sorts living beings today by who their ancestors were, using DNA as well as what can be seen. Whales end up beside cows, not beside fish.

explanations.art: The same eleven shapes drawn twice: once in a circle group and a square group, once in a red group and a blue group.

chart.title: The same shapes, sorted by colour

explanations.concept: Sorting does not change how many there are in all
explanations.context: In the Heap Test you counted the whole heap after every sort. This card says what you found.
explanations.definition: Sorting only moves things. If nothing is added and nothing is taken away, the number in all stays the same.
explanations.description: You had 15 things in the heap. You sorted them by kind and got 6, 5 and 4. Count them all together and it is still 15. You sorted them by colour and got 7, 5 and 3, and it is 15 again. The groups changed. The number in all did not. This is a good way to check your work. If the groups do not add up to the number you started with, something was missed or counted twice.
examples: 12 clothes in the wash basket are still 12 clothes when sorted into three piles.
20 children stand in two lines or four lines. There are still 20 children.
If your groups make 14 and the heap had 15, look under the plate for the lost one.

perspectives.explanation: Piaget's famous tests found that young children often think the number changes when things are spread out. They have not yet fixed the idea that moving does not change how many.
The number in a set is a fact about the set itself, not about how it is arranged. Spread out or heaped up, six things are still six.

explanations.art: Three groups of small things with an arrow showing them pushed back into one heap, labelled 15 both times.

chart.title: Three groups, one heap

explanations.context: This card shows how to keep count on paper. You used marks in the Heap Test and in the activity A Mark for Each.
explanations.definition: A mark is a short line that stands for one thing. One thing gets one mark.
explanations.description: Some things cannot be put in a pile. You cannot pile up the fans in your home, or the autos on the road. So you draw one mark for each. Here is a worked example. You see a fan and draw one mark beside the word fan. You see another fan and draw one more. At the end you count the marks. The marks stay on the paper, so you do not have to remember.
examples: A cricket scorer makes a mark in the book for every ball that is bowled.
A milk seller may mark the wall or a card each day she brings milk.
A table keeps the marks for each group in their own row, as in the picture.

perspectives.explanation: Notches cut on bones, such as the Ishango bone from Africa, may be some of the oldest tallies. One cut stands for one thing, which people have used for tens of thousands of years.
Many Chinese people tally in fives with the strokes of the character 正, while many Europeans cross four lines with a fifth. Different groups, same idea of one mark each.

explanations.art: A child holding a paper with a hand-drawn table, pointing a pencil at a ceiling fan.

chart.title: Things in one home, one mark for each

explanations.concept: When a thing is hard to place
explanations.context: In the Heap Test, one thing may not have fitted your groups well. This card says what sorters do then.
explanations.definition: If a thing fits two groups, or no group, the sorter decides where it goes and then does the same every time.
explanations.description: A clip that is half red and half blue is hard to sort by colour. A spoon made of wood and steel is hard to sort by what it is made of. Nothing is wrong with the thing. Your rule did not say what to do. So you add to the rule. You can say 'I go by the bigger part'. Or you can make a new group called 'two colours'. What matters is that you do the same every time, and that you can tell someone your rule.
examples: Is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable? Cooks say vegetable. Plant scientists say fruit.
A book about a dog on a train can go with animal books or train books. The librarian chooses.
A sock with no partner gets its own small group until the partner turns up.

perspectives.explanation: Biologists meet this all the time. Euglena is a tiny living being that has green chloroplasts like a plant and swims like an animal. Scientists had to decide where to put it, and the choice has changed over time.
He pointed out that the things we call games do not share one feature. They are linked by overlapping likenesses, like a family. Some things belong to a group without fitting a clean rule.

explanations.art: A clothes clip that is half red and half blue lying between a red group and a blue group, with a child looking puzzled.

chart.title: A yellow one turns up. The rule needs a new group.

explanations.context: People are not the only ones who sort. This card tells what scientists saw inside the nests of one kind of ant.
explanations.definition: Some ants keep their young sorted by size, in rings.
explanations.description: A small ant called Temnothorax lives in thin cracks in rocks. The ants keep all their young in one flat cluster. Two scientists, Nigel Franks and Ana Sendova-Franks, looked closely at these clusters and wrote about them in 1992. The eggs and the tiniest young were in the middle. Bigger young lay in rings around them, with the biggest furthest out. When the ants moved to a new nest, they laid their young out in the same way again. Why they sort like this is still an idea. The scientists think it may give each young ant the room and the care they need.
examples: Middle: eggs and the tiniest young. Next ring: small young. Outside ring: the biggest young.
Fox squirrels in America, given four kinds of nuts at one spot, buried each kind in its own area.
Watch the ants at home. Do they carry one kind of food and leave another?

perspectives.explanation: It looks as if the ants plan their rings, like someone tidying a room.

perspectives.who: Researchers who study these ants (Franks and Deneubourg)
perspectives.explanation: No ant needs a plan. Each ant follows simple local rules, and the rings come out of many ants doing this together.

explanations.art: A top view of an ant nest in a flat crack: tiny eggs in the middle, small larvae in a ring around them and large larvae in an outer ring, with worker ants walking between.

chart.title: How the ants lay out their young (the numbers are only an example)

explanations.concept: Sorting helps us understand the world
explanations.context: Sorting is not only for toys and spoons. This card shows how sorting and counting help people understand very big things.
explanations.definition: People sort and count to find out what is there and how much of each.
explanations.description: A shop sorts so that you can find the rice. Scientists sort too. About a hundred years ago, an American scientist named Annie Jump Cannon sorted the stars. She looked at the light of each star and put the star in a group. Hot blue-white stars went at one end and cooler red stars at the other. She sorted about 350,000 stars. People who study stars still use her groups today. Once the stars were sorted, people could count each group and ask why some kinds are rare.
examples: A doctor sorts blood into groups called A, B, AB and O before giving blood to a sick person.
Waste is sorted into wet and dry so that each kind can be used again.
A post office sorts letters by the place they are going to.

perspectives.explanation: The Greek thinker Aristotle sorted animals by how they live and breed. He believed sorting is how we find the order of nature.
Some biologists remind us that nature is a smooth spread, and the lines between groups are ones we draw. Sorting is a tool for thinking, not a list that nature handed us.

explanations.art: A woman from the early 1900s at a desk looking at a glass photograph of stars through a magnifying glass, with a notebook of letters beside her.

chart.title: Stars sorted by their light (a simple picture, not real numbers)

agreed.text: If you only move things into groups, the number of things in all stays the same.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it. Count a heap, sort it, and count all the groups together. The Heap Test does this three times.

agreed.text: The same things can be sorted by more than one rule, and each rule gives different groups.
agreed.evidence: Sort clothes clips by colour and then by size. The groups change, but the clips do not.

agreed.text: People were making marks to keep count a very long time before they could write.
agreed.evidence: A bone with 29 cut marks was found in Border Cave, in southern Africa. It is about 42,000 years old. Nobody knows what its maker was counting.

agreed.text: Some other animals sort things too.
agreed.evidence: In 1992, scientists reported that Temnothorax ants keep their young sorted by size, in rings. In 2017, scientists reported that fox squirrels can bury each kind of nut in its own area.

challenging.claim: There is one right way to sort a heap of things.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief: that a heap of things has one correct way to be sorted.
challenging.for: At home and in school we are often shown one way, such as spoons with spoons. For that job it is the best way.
challenging.against: The same heap can be sorted by kind, colour, size or what it is made of. Each sort is right for a different question.

challenging.claim: The group that takes up the most room has the most things.
challenging.context: This card is about judging a group by how big it looks, not by counting.
challenging.for: Often a bigger heap does have more things in it, so the guess works some of the time.
challenging.against: Three big brinjals take up more room than six small lemons. Only counting, or matching one to one, tells you which group has more.

challenging.claim: Some groups are made by nature, not by people.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument: do we make all our groups, or are some groups already there?
challenging.for: A crow's chicks are always crows, never sparrows. Gold is gold wherever you find it. These groups seem to be there before anyone sorts.
challenging.against: Even scientists often disagree about where one kind of living being ends and the next begins. And we still choose which likeness to sort by.

big_questions.q: You sort a heap two ways and get different groups. Which sort is the right one?
big_questions.hint: What did you want to find out each time?

big_questions.q: Can a thing belong to two groups at once? Can you?
big_questions.hint: Think of a red spoon. Then think of yourself: a child, a cousin, a singer.

big_questions.q: If you sort the heap ten different ways, will the number in all ever change?
big_questions.hint: Did you add any? Did you take any away?

big_questions.q: Who decided that a tomato is a vegetable? Could it have been decided another way?
big_questions.hint: Ask a cook. Then look inside a tomato for seeds.

big_questions.q: Ants sort their young by size. Do they choose their rule the way you choose yours?
big_questions.hint: Nobody knows yet. What could you watch for?

big_questions.q: Is there anything in the world that cannot be put in any group?
big_questions.hint: Try to think of one. Then ask: is 'things with no group' a group?

story.title: The Stairway Library
story.note: Nila, Kathir, Fathima Aunty and the library are made up. Mylapore is a real part of Chennai.
text: Nila was seven. She lived on the second floor of a yellow building in Mylapore, in Chennai. On the landing outside her door stood an old shoe rack. It had no shoes on it. It had books.
This was Nila's library. Any child in the building could take a book home. They only had to bring it back.
On Saturday morning the books came back all at once. Eighteen of them lay in one heap on the landing.
'I will put them away nicely,' said Nila.
She put the tall books on the bottom shelf. She put the middle-sized books on the middle shelf. She put the small books on the top shelf. Nothing stuck out and nothing fell over. Nila was pleased.
Then Kathir came down the stairs. Kathir was five, and he lived on the third floor.
'Akka, do you have more animal books or more train books?' he asked. 'I want the kind you have the most of.'
Nila looked at her shelves. Tall, middle, small. She could not tell.

'Wait,' she said. She began to count the animal books with her finger. There was a cat book on the top shelf. There was a tiger book on the bottom shelf. Was that an elephant on the middle shelf? Had she counted the cat already? She lost her place and had to start again. Then she lost her place again.
'You sorted them the wrong way,' said Kathir.
'It is not wrong,' said Nila. 'It is a good way to make them stand up.' She thought for a moment. 'But it does not help with your question. Your question needs a different sort.'

She took all eighteen books down again. This time she did not look at how big they were. She looked at what each book was about. Animal books went here. Train and bus books went there. Books about people went in a third pile.
At the end, one book was left in her hand. It was about a dog who rides a train.
'Animal,' said Kathir.
'Train,' said Nila.
They looked at each other.

'It is my library,' said Nila slowly, 'so I have to choose. But I must choose the same way every time, or nobody will find anything.' She looked at the cover. The dog was big and the train was small. 'If an animal is the main one in the story, the book goes with the animal books.' She put the book on the animal pile.
Kathir nodded. That was fair.

Now the counting was easy. Nila found a piece of chalk. On the wall she drew a cat face, a train and a smiling face. She touched the first animal book and made one mark next to the cat. She touched the next one and made another mark. One book, one mark.
Kathir wanted the chalk, so he did the trains. Nila did the people books.
When they had finished, there were eight marks next to the cat. There were four marks next to the train. There were six marks next to the smiling face.
'Animals!' said Kathir. He had not even counted. The line of marks next to the cat was the longest. He took the tiger book and sat down on the stairs to look at it.
A little later Fathima Aunty came up from the ground floor. Her small daughter Sana was holding her hand.
'Nila, which of your books are thin?' she asked. 'Sana can only sit still for a thin book.'
Kathir looked up from his tiger. He looked at the three piles. Animals, trains, people. He began to laugh. 'Akka, now they are sorted the wrong way again!'
Nila laughed too. This time she did not mind at all. She had worked it out. The books did not have one right place. They had a right place for each question.
She went through the three piles and pulled out every thin book. It did not take long. 'Five thin books, Aunty. Sana can choose.'

That evening Nila put the books back on the shoe rack. She thought for a long time about how to do it. In the end she sorted them by what they were about, because that was what children asked most often.
She left the chalk marks on the wall. Next Saturday the books would come back in a heap again. Somebody would ask a new question. Then she would take the books down and sort them once more.
story.epiphany: For the parent: there is no single right way to sort. The right sort is the one that answers the question being asked. A hard case, like the dog on the train, needs a decision that is then kept the same every time. And one mark for each thing lets a child compare groups without holding numbers in her head.
ask: Why could Nila not answer Kathir's question from her neat shelves?
The book about a dog on a train fits two piles. Where would you put it? Why?
Kathir knew which pile had the most without counting. How?
How would you sort your own books? What question would that sort answer?

experiments.title: The Heap Test: one heap, three ways to sort
experiments.context: In this test you sort one heap of 15 small things three times, by three different rules. Before each sort you guess what the biggest group will be. You will find out what a new rule changes and what it cannot change.
experiments.question: If we sort the same heap by a new rule, do the groups change? Does the number of things in all change?
experiments.predict: Before each sort, guess which group will be the biggest. Guess whether there will still be 15 things in all. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same 15 things every time. Nobody adds a thing or takes one away. After every sort we count each group, and then we count them all together.
results_table: My guess for the biggest group
The groups and how many in each

materials.item: small things in 3 kinds and 3 or more colours, such as clothes clips, crayons and bottle lids
materials.qty: 15 in all, in unequal numbers (for example 6, 5 and 4)

materials.item: sheets of paper or steel plates to hold the groups
a paper and a pencil for the table

experiments.safety: Keep small things such as buttons, lids and beans away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Count a heap of 15 things. Sort it by kind, by colour and by your own rule. Count the groups and the whole heap each time.

experiments.record: A grown-up draws the table. For each rule, write the guess, then draw one mark for each thing next to its group. Write how many in all. At the end the child says what they found, and the grown-up writes it under the table.

example_chart.title: What a finished table can look like (your things and numbers will be your own)

setup.art: Fifteen mixed clothes clips, crayons and bottle lids in a jumbled heap on a floor, with four empty sheets of paper beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Make one heap of 15 things. Count them.

setup.art: The same things sorted on three sheets of paper: clips on one, crayons on one, lids on one, with a child counting the clips.
setup.caption: 2. Sort by kind. Count each group.

setup.art: The same things sorted again on three sheets by colour: red things, blue things and yellow things, clips, crayons and lids mixed in each.
setup.caption: 3. Mix them up. Sort by colour. Count again.

flow.do: 1. Put the 15 things in one mixed heap. 2. Ask which kind there is most of, by looking only. 3. Write the guess. 4. Your child counts the whole heap, moving each thing.
flow.say: Look, but do not touch. Which kind is there most of? Why do you think so? Now count them all.
flow.kid: Look at the heap. Which kind is there most of? Guess. Then count them all.

ask.q: Why is it hard to tell which kind there is most of?
good: The lids are big, so they look like more.

flow.parent: Do not say the numbers of each kind. The heap should hold 15 things. If your child's count is different, count again together, moving each thing aside.

chart.title: A mixed heap can look like this

flow.context: This is the first step of the Heap Test. You look at a mixed heap of 15 things, guess which kind there is most of, and count the whole heap.

flow.do: 1. Lay out three sheets of paper. 2. Ask your child to put each kind on its own sheet. 3. Your child counts each group. 4. Draw one mark for each thing in the table. 5. Ask which group has the most and the fewest.
flow.say: Put things that are the same kind together. Then count each group. Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Put each kind on its own paper. Count each group. Draw one mark for each thing.

ask.q: Which group has the most? Which has the fewest?
good: There are 6 clips and only 4 lids.

flow.parent: Let your child name the groups. If the guess from step 1 was wrong, that is useful. Ask what made the other kind look like more.

chart.title: An example heap, sorted by kind

flow.context: This is step 2 of the Heap Test. You sort the heap of 15 things by kind and count each group.

flow.do: 1. Ask how many things there are in all now, before counting. 2. Ask for a reason. 3. Push the groups together and count them all. 4. Write the number in the table.
flow.say: We made three groups. How many things are there in all now? More than 15, fewer, or still 15? Why?
flow.kid: You made three groups. How many things in all now? Guess. Then count them all.
flow.parent: Some children expect a new number, because the heap looks different now. Let the count answer.

chart.title: The example heap, sorted by kind

flow.context: This is step 3 of the Heap Test. After sorting the heap by kind, you check how many things there are in all.

flow.do: 1. Mix the heap again. 2. Say the new rule: colour. 3. Ask which colour group will be the biggest, and why. 4. Your child sorts by colour and counts each group. 5. Draw the marks and count them all.
flow.say: New rule: sort by colour. Which colour group will be the biggest? Why? Will there still be 15?
flow.kid: Mix them up. Now sort by colour. Count each group. Then count them all.

ask.q: What is different from the first sort? What is the same?
good: Now clips and lids are together.
A different group is the biggest.

flow.parent: Clips, crayons and lids now share groups. If a thing has two colours, let your child decide where it goes. Ask them to say their reason.

chart.title: The same example heap, sorted by colour

flow.context: This is step 4 of the Heap Test. You mix the same 15 things again and sort them by colour.

flow.do: 1. Mix the heap again. 2. Ask your child to think of a new rule and keep it secret. 3. Your child sorts. 4. You guess the rule. 5. Count each group and count them all.
flow.say: Now you choose the rule. Do not tell me. Sort them, and I will guess your rule.
flow.kid: Think of your own rule. Keep it secret. Sort the heap. Can your grown-up guess it?

ask.q: What was your rule? Did every thing fit a group?
good: Things that roll and things that do not.
This one did not fit, so I made a new group.

flow.parent: Any rule is fine if your child can say it and uses it the same way for every thing. Ideas if they are stuck: big and small, rolls or does not roll, what it is made of.
flow.context: This is step 5 of the Heap Test. You sort the same 15 things by a rule you make up yourself.

flow.do: 1. Pick the thing that was hardest to place. 2. Ask where it went and why. 3. Ask whether it could have gone in another group.
flow.say: Which thing was the hardest to place? Where did you put it? Could it go somewhere else?
flow.kid: Which thing was hard to place? Where did you put it? Say why.
flow.parent: If nothing was hard, show a thing with two colours or two materials and ask where it would go. The point is that the sorter decides, and then keeps to it.
flow.context: This is step 6 of the Heap Test. You talk about the one thing that was hardest to place in a group.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask what changed from sort to sort, and what did not. 3. Ask why. 4. Write your child's words under the table.
flow.say: Look at our table. What changed each time we sorted? What never changed? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at your table. What changed each time? What stayed the same?

ask.q: What do you think now? What did you see? Why is it so?
good: The groups changed when the rule changed.
The biggest group was different each time.
Because we only moved them. We did not add any.

check.q: You sort 12 buttons by colour. Then you mix them and sort them by size. How many buttons in all now?
check.why: Still 12. Sorting only moves the buttons. No button was added or taken away. Picking another answer often means the new groups looked bigger or smaller. Count them to check.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Heap Test. You look at the table and say what a new sorting rule changes and what it does not.

activities.title: Line Them Up: see the most without counting
activities.context: In this activity you lay three groups of kitchen things in rows on the floor, one thing in each floor tile. The point is to see which group has the most, and how many more, by matching one to one.
activities.problem: Can you tell which group has the most without counting?

materials.item: three kinds of kitchen things, such as spoons, steel tumblers and lids
materials.qty: 4 to 8 of each kind, in unequal numbers

materials.item: a tiled floor, or a paper with a row of boxes drawn for each kind

schedule.what: Lay three groups in rows, one thing in each tile. Find the longest row and how many more it has.

activities.record: Draw the three rows on paper as dots, one dot for each thing. Circle the longest row.

setup.art: Spoons, steel tumblers and lids in three small heaps beside a tiled floor.
setup.caption: 1. Sort the things into three groups.

setup.art: Three rows on floor tiles starting at the same wall: six spoons, four tumblers and five lids, one thing in each tile.
setup.caption: 2. Lay each group in a row. One thing in each tile.

setup.art: A child pointing at the two spoons that stick out past the end of the row of tumblers.
setup.caption: 3. The longest row has the most. Count what sticks out.

flow.do: 1. Sort the things into three groups. 2. Ask your child to lay each group in a row, any way they like. 3. Ask which row has the most.
flow.say: Put each group in a row. Which row has the most? How do you know?
flow.kid: Put each group in a row. Which row has the most?
flow.parent: Your child may spread one row out and squash another. Then the longest row may not have the most. Let this happen. The next step sorts it out.

chart.title: An example: one thing in each tile

flow.context: This is the first step of Line Them Up. You lay three groups of kitchen things in rows and say which has the most.

flow.do: 1. Start all three rows at the same wall or line. 2. Put one thing in each floor tile. 3. Ask again which row has the most. 4. Check by counting.
flow.say: This time, one thing in each tile. All rows start at the wall. Now which has the most?
flow.kid: Start each row at the wall. Put one thing in each tile. Which row is longest?

ask.q: Why does each thing need its own tile?

flow.parent: With one thing in each tile, the longest row really does have the most. Without tiles, a few big tumblers can make a longer row than many spoons.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Line Them Up. You lay each group in a row with one thing in each floor tile, so the rows can be compared.

flow.do: 1. Point to the longest row and one other row. 2. Ask how many more the longer row has. 3. Show how to count only the things that stick out.
flow.say: How many more spoons than tumblers? Count only the ones that stick out past the tumblers.
flow.kid: Look at two rows. Count the things that stick out. That is how many more.

check.q: A row of 6 spoons lies next to a row of 4 tumblers, one in each tile. How many spoons stick out?
check.why: 2 spoons stick out. Four spoons each have a tumbler next to them. Two do not. So there are 2 more spoons than tumblers. Picking 6 means counting the whole row.

flow.context: This is the last step of Line Them Up. You find how many more one row has by counting what sticks out.

activities.title: Sort the Washing: whose pile is the biggest?
activities.context: This is a real job with real maths in it. You sort the family's dry clothes by person, count each pile, then sort them again by kind. The point is to see how one pile of washing answers two different questions.
activities.problem: The dry clothes are in one heap. Who has the most clothes in this wash? And how many pieces must go to be ironed?

materials.item: one load of dry, clean clothes, 12 to 20 pieces
a bed or a clean mat to sort on

schedule.what: Sort the dry washing by person and count each pile. Sort again by kind. Make the list for ironing.

activities.record: Write each person's name with one mark for each piece of clothing. Circle the name with the most marks.

setup.art: A heap of dry clothes on a bed: shirts, a sari, shorts, towels and socks, with a child standing beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Tip the dry clothes on the bed. Count the pieces.

setup.art: The clothes sorted into four piles on the bed, each with a name slip: Amma, Appa, Paatti and the child.
setup.caption: 2. Sort by person. Count each pile.

setup.art: The same clothes sorted again into shirts, shorts, towels and socks, with a paper list beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Sort again by kind. Write the list for ironing.

flow.do: 1. Tip the dry clothes onto the bed. 2. Ask who has the most clothes in this wash, by looking. 3. Your child counts all the pieces. A pair of socks counts as one piece.
flow.say: Who do you think has the most clothes in this wash? Now count all the pieces.
flow.kid: Look at the heap. Who has the most clothes here? Guess. Then count every piece.
flow.parent: Put each pair of socks together first, so that a pair is one piece. Write the number in all at the top of the paper.

chart.title: An example wash

flow.context: This is the first step of Sort the Washing. You guess who has the most clothes in the wash, and count all the pieces.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to make one pile for each person. 2. Write each name on the paper. 3. Your child draws one mark for each piece beside the right name. 4. Count the marks.
flow.say: Make one pile for each of us. Then draw one mark for each piece, next to the name.
flow.kid: Make a pile for each person. Draw one mark for each piece of clothing.

ask.q: Who has the most? Who has the fewest? Do all the piles together still make the first number?

flow.parent: A towel that everyone uses fits no pile. Let your child decide: a pile called 'everyone' is a good answer.

chart.title: An example: one mark for each piece

flow.context: This is step 2 of Sort the Washing. You sort the dry clothes by person and draw one mark for each piece.

flow.do: 1. Say that the clothes now need to be put away. 2. Ask your child to sort the same clothes by kind. 3. Count each kind. 4. Count all the pieces again.
flow.say: Now we sort a new way. All the shirts together, all the towels together. How many of each kind?
flow.kid: Now sort by kind. Shirts with shirts. Towels with towels. Count each kind.

ask.q: Which sort helps us know whose is whose? Which sort helps with ironing?
good: By person, for whose it is.
It depends what we want to do.

flow.parent: Both sorts are useful. The first tells each person what is theirs. The second shows how many shirts need ironing.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Sort the Washing. You sort the same dry clothes again, this time by kind.

flow.do: 1. Pick out the pieces that need ironing. 2. Your child counts them. 3. Write the number on a slip for the ironing shop or the person who irons at home.
flow.say: The ironing person charges for each piece. How many pieces are we sending?
flow.kid: Pick out the clothes for ironing. Count them. Write the number on a slip.
flow.parent: Ironing shops in India usually charge for each piece, so they count the pieces too. If you iron at home, the count still tells you how big the job is.

check.q: 14 clothes are sorted by person. Then the same clothes are sorted by kind. How many clothes are there now?
check.why: 14. They are the same clothes, sorted a new way. Picking 28 means counting each piece once for each sort.

flow.context: This is the last step of Sort the Washing. You count the pieces that need ironing and write the number down.

activities.title: A Mark for Each: count the things you cannot pile up
activities.context: In this activity you walk through your home and count the fans, doors, windows and taps. You cannot put them in a pile, so you draw one mark for each. The point is to learn to keep count on paper.
activities.problem: How many fans, doors, windows and taps are there in your home? Which are there most of?

materials.item: paper on a hard book or board

schedule.what: Draw a table with four rows. Walk through the home and draw one mark for each fan, door, window and tap. Count the marks.

activities.record: Keep the table. Write the number at the end of each row. Circle the row with the most marks.

setup.art: A paper with a hand-drawn table of four rows, each starting with a small drawing: a fan, a door, a window and a tap.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table. One row for each kind of thing.

setup.art: A child standing in a room, looking up at a ceiling fan and drawing a mark on the paper.
setup.caption: 2. Walk through your home. One thing, one mark.

setup.art: The finished table with marks in each row and a number written at the end of each row.
setup.caption: 3. Count the marks in each row.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with four rows. 2. At the start of each row, draw a fan, a door, a window and a tap. 3. Ask your child to guess which row will get the most marks.
flow.say: We will count four kinds of things at home. Which do you think we have the most of? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the four rows. Which thing do you have most of at home? Guess.

chart.title: The table before you start

flow.context: This is the first step of A Mark for Each. You make a table for the fans, doors, windows and taps in your home, and guess which row will have the most marks.

flow.do: 1. Walk through the home together, room by room. 2. Each time your child sees a fan, door, window or tap, they draw one mark in its row. 3. Finish each room before going to the next.
flow.say: Each time you see one, draw one mark in its row. One thing, one mark.
flow.kid: Walk through each room. See a fan? Draw one mark. One thing, one mark.

ask.q: How do you make sure you do not mark the same door twice?
good: Touch it when I mark it.

flow.parent: Going room by room, in one direction, stops double counting. A door between two rooms gets one mark, not two.
flow.context: This is step 2 of A Mark for Each. You walk through your home and draw one mark for each fan, door, window and tap.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts the marks in each row and writes the number. 2. Ask which row has the most and which has the fewest. 3. Compare with the guess.
flow.say: Count the marks in each row. Which thing do we have the most of? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Count the marks in each row. Write the number. Which row has the most?

check.q: The row for doors has these marks: | | | | |. How many doors is that?
check.why: 5 doors. Each mark stands for one door, and there are five marks. Picking 1 means reading the whole row as one thing.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Mark for Each. You count the marks for the fans, doors, windows and taps, and find which there is most of.

activities.title: Pick the Dal Clean: sorting in the kitchen
activities.context: In many kitchens, people spread rice or dal on a plate and pick out anything that should not be cooked. That is sorting. In this activity you sort a mixed spoonful of three dals and count each kind. The point is to see sorting as part of cooking.
activities.problem: Three kinds of dal are mixed up on one plate. Can you get each kind back into its own bowl?

materials.item: three kinds of dal or beans that look different, such as rajma, white chana and green moong

activities.safety: Wash your hands first, so that the dal can be cooked afterwards. Keep small things such as buttons, lids and beans away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Mix three spoons of dal on a plate. Sort them into three bowls by sliding. Count each kind.

activities.record: Draw three bowls. Write how many of each kind you found. Circle the bowl with the most.

setup.art: A steel plate with a small mixed heap of rajma, white chana and green moong, and three empty katoris beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Mix one spoon of each dal on a plate.

setup.art: A child's finger sliding one rajma bean to the edge of the plate towards a katori.
setup.caption: 2. Slide each one to its own bowl.

setup.art: Three katoris, each holding one kind of dal, with a number written on a slip in front of each.
setup.caption: 3. Count each kind. Which bowl has the most?

flow.do: 1. Wash hands. 2. Put one small spoon of each dal on the plate and mix them. 3. Ask which kind there is most of, by looking.
flow.say: I put in one spoon of each. Do you think there is the same number of each kind? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the mixed dal. Is there the same number of each kind? Guess.
flow.parent: One spoon holds far fewer big rajma than small moong. Do not say so yet.

chart.title: An example of what one spoon of each can hold

flow.context: This is the first step of Pick the Dal Clean. Three kinds of dal are mixed on a plate, and you guess whether there is the same number of each.

flow.do: 1. Your child slides each dal, one at a time, into its own bowl. 2. Watch for any that are broken or odd. 3. Ask where those should go.
flow.say: Slide each one to its own bowl. What will you do with a broken one?
flow.kid: Slide each dal to its own bowl. One at a time. What about broken ones?
flow.parent: A broken or spoiled piece fits none of the three bowls. A fourth group, 'not for cooking', is how cooks deal with it.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Pick the Dal Clean. You sort the mixed dal into three bowls, one kind in each.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts each bowl. 2. Write the numbers. 3. Ask which has the most and why one spoon gave different numbers.
flow.say: Count each bowl. One spoon of each, but the numbers are different. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Count each bowl. Which kind has the most? Why are the numbers different?

ask.q: Why did one spoon of moong hold more than one spoon of rajma?
good: More small ones fit in a spoon.

check.q: One spoon holds 6 rajma. The same spoon holds 14 moong. Which is true?
options: Each moong is smaller than each rajma
check.why: Each moong is smaller, so more of them fit in the same spoon. The same amount of room can hold different numbers of things.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pick the Dal Clean. You count each kind of dal and think about why one spoon of each gave different numbers.

activities.title: Ant Watch: what do the ants choose?
activities.context: Ants sort food as they collect it: they carry some kinds away and leave others. In this activity you offer ants two foods and make one mark for each ant who carries each kind. Do this only if you have ants on a balcony, a window sill or outside. If no ants come, try another day.
activities.problem: You put out sugar and rava side by side. Which do your ants carry away more?

materials.item: a pinch of sugar and a pinch of rava (or broken rice)
a place where ants walk, such as a balcony corner or a window sill

activities.safety: Watch the ants without touching them. Some ants bite. Do not put food where you do not want ants to come.

schedule.what: Put sugar and rava near an ant trail. Wait about 10 minutes. Then watch for 5 minutes and make one mark for each ant who carries each food.

activities.record: Keep your table of marks. Write which food got more marks. Write one thing you saw an ant do.

setup.art: Two small pinches of food a hand-width apart on a balcony floor near a line of ants: white sugar grains and yellowish rava.
setup.caption: 1. Put a pinch of sugar and a pinch of rava near the ants.

setup.art: A child crouching at a distance with a paper and pencil, watching ants carry grains away.
setup.caption: 2. Watch. One mark for each ant who carries a grain.

setup.art: A paper with two rows, 'sugar' and 'rava', and pencil marks beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Count the marks. Which did the ants choose more?

flow.do: 1. Put a pinch of sugar and a pinch of rava a hand-width apart, near where ants walk. 2. Draw a table with two rows. 3. Ask for a guess. 4. Wait about 10 minutes for the ants to find the food.
flow.say: Which will the ants carry away more, sugar or rava? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put out the sugar and the rava. Which will the ants take more? Guess. Then wait 10 minutes.
flow.parent: Different kinds of ants like different foods, so the result is not the same in every home. While you wait, your child can draw an ant.

chart.title: Your table before you start

flow.context: This is the first step of Ant Watch. You put sugar and rava near some ants and guess which they will carry away more.

flow.do: 1. Watch for 5 minutes. 2. Each time an ant carries a grain away, your child draws one mark in that food's row. 3. Do not touch the ants.
flow.say: Each time an ant carries a grain away, draw one mark in the right row.
flow.kid: Watch the ants. An ant carries a grain away? Draw one mark.
flow.parent: The ants will not wait for your child, so marks are the only way to keep count. It is fine to miss one or two.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Ant Watch. You watch ants at two foods and draw one mark for each ant who carries a grain away.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts the marks in each row. 2. Ask which food the ants chose more. 3. Ask what else they noticed.
flow.say: Count your marks. Which food did the ants choose more? What else did you see them do?
flow.kid: Count the marks in each row. Which food did the ants choose more?

ask.q: How do you think an ant tells sugar from rava?
good: They touch it with their feelers.

check.q: Your table shows 7 marks for sugar and 2 marks for rava. What does it tell you?
check.why: More ants carried sugar. Each mark is one ant carrying one grain, and 7 is more than 2. In all you saw 9 grains carried, not 7.

flow.context: This is the last step of Ant Watch. You count your marks and say which food the ants carried away more.

games.title: Guess My Rule
games.players: 2 or more players: with a parent or with friends. One player can play the sorting puzzle in the last rule alone.
games.context: This is a card game with 12 shape cards. One player sorts the cards by a secret rule, and the others guess the rule. It builds the habit of asking: in what way are these alike?

printables.title: 12 shape cards to draw, colour and cut out

rules: Make the 12 cards. On each one, draw and colour the shape that its words say. Mix the cards and lay them face up.
The sorter thinks of a secret rule. It can be a colour, a shape or a size: for example 'red ones', 'triangles' or 'big ones'.
The sorter picks up one card at a time. A card that fits the rule goes on the YES pile. A card that does not fit goes on the NO pile.
After each card, the guesser may make one guess at the rule. The sorter says only 'yes' or 'not yet'.
When the guess is right, count the cards in the YES and NO piles together. That is the guesser's score. A low score is good.
Swap jobs. After two rounds each, the player with the lowest score in all wins.
Playing alone: lay out all 12 cards. Sort them by colour, then by shape, then by size. Each time, count the groups and the cards in each group.

setup.art: Twelve hand-drawn cards face up on a floor: big and small circles, squares and triangles, in red and blue.
setup.caption: 1. Make the 12 cards. Lay them face up.

setup.art: Two piles labelled YES and NO, with a big red circle and a small red square on YES and a big blue circle on NO.
setup.caption: 2. The sorter puts each card on YES or NO.

setup.art: A child pointing at the YES pile and saying 'Red ones!', while the other player nods.
setup.caption: 3. Guess the rule. Fewer cards is better.

flow.do: 1. Make the 12 cards together. 2. Lay them face up. 3. Ask your child to name three ways the cards differ.
flow.say: Look at the cards. In what ways are they different from each other?
flow.kid: Lay out the 12 cards. How are they different? Find three ways.

ask.q: In what ways do the cards differ?

chart.title: Each shape comes in red and blue, and in a big and a small size

flow.context: This is the first step of Guess My Rule, a card game where one player sorts shape cards by a secret rule. Here you make the cards and look at how they differ.

flow.do: 1. You are the sorter first. 2. Choose the rule 'red ones'. 3. Place cards one at a time on YES or NO. 4. After each card, your child guesses.
flow.say: I have a secret rule. This card goes on YES. This one goes on NO. What is my rule?
flow.kid: Watch the YES pile and the NO pile. What is the secret rule? Guess.
flow.parent: Start with a colour rule, which is the easiest to see. Then try a shape, then a size.

check.q: A big red circle and a small red square are on YES. A big blue circle is on NO. Which rule fits?
check.why: Red ones. Both YES cards are red and the NO card is blue. It cannot be 'circles' or 'big ones', because a big circle is on the NO pile.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Guess My Rule, a card game where one player sorts shape cards by a secret rule. Here the grown-up sorts and the child guesses.

flow.do: 1. Swap jobs. 2. Your child chooses a secret rule and sorts. 3. You guess after each card. 4. Count the cards used.
flow.say: Now you are the sorter. Think of a rule. Do not tell me. I will guess.
flow.kid: Now you sort. Think of a secret rule. Put each card on YES or NO.
flow.parent: If a card lands on the wrong pile, do not correct it at once. Ask your child to say the rule at the end and check each card together.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Guess My Rule, a card game where one player sorts shape cards by a secret rule. Here the child sorts and the grown-up guesses.

flow.do: 1. Add up each player's scores. 2. The lowest score wins. 3. Ask which rule was the hardest to guess.
flow.say: Who used the fewest cards? Which rule was the hardest to guess? Why?
flow.kid: Add up your scores. The lowest score wins. Which rule was hardest?
flow.context: This is the last step of Guess My Rule, a card game where one player sorts shape cards by a secret rule. Here you add the scores and find the winner.

games.title: Roll and Mark
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a dice game played on a sheet with six rows, one for each number on the dice. Every roll gets one mark. It builds quick marking, and counting and comparing of groups.

printables.title: A Roll and Mark sheet: six rows with five boxes in each

rules: Draw the sheet: six rows, numbered 1 to 6, with five boxes in each row.
Before the game, each player picks one number from 1 to 6 as their own. No two players pick the same number.
Take turns to roll the dice. Whatever number comes up, draw one mark in a box of that number's row.
The first row to fill all five boxes wins the race. If that row is your number, you win. If it is nobody's number, nobody wins that race.
After the race, count the marks in each row. Say which number came up the most and which came up the fewest.
Playing alone: guess which number will win, then roll and mark. Play three races. Does the same number win every time?

setup.art: A hand-drawn sheet with six rows numbered 1 to 6, five empty boxes in each row, a dice and a pencil beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw six rows of five boxes. Pick your number.

setup.art: A dice showing 4 and a child's hand drawing a mark in the first box of row 4.
setup.caption: 2. Roll. Draw one mark in that number's row.

setup.art: The sheet with row 2 completely filled with five marks and other rows partly filled, with a child cheering.
setup.caption: 3. The first row to fill five boxes wins.

flow.do: 1. Draw the sheet. 2. Each player picks a number and writes their name beside its row. 3. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Pick your number. Each time the dice shows a number, that row gets one mark.
flow.kid: Draw six rows. Each row has five boxes. Pick your number.

chart.title: The Roll and Mark sheet

flow.context: This is the first step of Roll and Mark, a dice game where every roll gets one mark on a sheet. Here you draw the sheet and pick a number.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll. 2. The roller draws one mark in the row of the number rolled. 3. Stop when one row has five marks.
flow.say: You rolled a 4. Which row gets the mark? One roll, one mark.
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Draw one mark in that number's row. One roll, one mark.
flow.parent: A race takes at most 25 rolls and usually fewer. Now and then ask which row is ahead and how many more it needs.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Roll and Mark, a dice game where every roll gets one mark on a sheet. Here you play until one row has five marks.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts the marks in each row and writes the number at the end. 2. Ask which number came up the most and the fewest. 3. Ask how many rolls there were in all.
flow.say: Count the marks in each row. Which number came up the most? How many times did we roll in all?
flow.kid: Count the marks in each row. Which number came up most? Which came up fewest?

ask.q: How can we find out how many rolls there were, without rolling again?

check.q: In a race, the row for 3 has 5 marks and the row for 6 has 2 marks. Which number came up more often?
check.why: 3 came up more often. Each mark is one roll, and 5 marks are more than 2 marks. Picking 6 means choosing the bigger number on the dice, not the bigger number of marks.

chart.title: An example race

flow.context: This is the last step of Roll and Mark, a dice game where every roll gets one mark on a sheet. Here you count the marks in each row.

projects.title: Sorting Week: one small sort every day
projects.context: In this five-day project you sort one real thing at home each day, for about five minutes. Each day you choose the rule, count the groups and draw the marks. It makes sorting and counting a daily habit.
projects.problem: A home is full of mixed-up things. Sort one of them each day, and find out what you have the most of.

materials.item: a notebook or five sheets of paper
things already at home: the spoon drawer, the shoe rack, a pencil box, the vegetable basket, your own toys

projects.safety: A grown-up takes knives and other sharp things out of the drawer before the child sorts it.

schedule.what: The spoon drawer. Sort by kind: big spoons, small spoons, ladles. Draw one mark for each.
The shoe rack. Sort by whose they are. Count the pairs in each group.
A pencil box or crayon box. Sort by colour, then by long and short.
The vegetable basket. Choose your own rule. Ask someone to guess it.
Your own toys or books. Sort them two ways. Tell someone which sort you like better and why.

projects.record: Each day, write the rule at the top of a page. Draw a small picture for each group and one mark for each thing. Circle the group with the most.

setup.art: An open kitchen drawer of mixed steel spoons and ladles, with a child looking in.
setup.caption: 1. Each day, pick one thing to sort.

setup.art: Big spoons, small spoons and ladles laid in three groups on a counter.
setup.caption: 2. Choose a rule. Sort. Count each group.

setup.art: A notebook page with the word 'spoons', three small drawings and pencil marks beside each, one group circled.
setup.caption: 3. Draw one mark for each. Circle the most.

flow.do: 1. Take the sharp things out of the spoon drawer. 2. Your child sorts the rest by kind. 3. Your child draws one mark for each spoon beside its group. 4. Circle the group with the most.
flow.say: Today we sort the spoon drawer. What groups will you make?
flow.kid: Sort the spoons by kind. Draw one mark for each. Circle the biggest group.

chart.title: A page from the notebook can look like this

flow.context: This is day 1 of Sorting Week, a five-day project where you sort one thing at home each day. Today you sort the spoon drawer.

flow.do: 1. On days 2, 3 and 4, sort the shoe rack, a pencil box and the vegetable basket. 2. Each day your child says the rule first. 3. Then they sort, count and draw the marks.
flow.say: What is today's rule? Say it first. Then sort and count.
flow.kid: Say your rule first. Then sort. Count each group. Draw your marks.

ask.q: Was there a thing today that was hard to place? What did you decide?
good: The tomato: I put it with the vegetables.

flow.parent: Five minutes a day is enough. On the shoe rack, the group to count can be pairs, not single shoes.
flow.context: These are days 2 to 4 of Sorting Week, a five-day project where you sort one thing at home each day. You sort shoes, pencils and vegetables.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, your child sorts their own toys or books two different ways. 2. They draw the marks for both sorts. 3. They tell someone which sort they like better, and why.
flow.say: Sort your own things two ways today. Which way do you like better? Why?
flow.kid: Sort your toys two ways. Draw the marks. Which way do you like better?

ask.q: Did both sorts have the same number in all?
good: Yes, they are the same toys.

check.q: You sort 9 toys by colour, and then the same 9 toys by size. What stays the same?
options: The number of toys in all
check.why: The number of toys in all stays at 9. The groups, and which group is the biggest, can both change when the rule changes.

flow.context: This is day 5 of Sorting Week, a five-day project where you sort one thing at home each day. Today you sort your own things in two ways.

challenges.title: Stretch: count what will not stay still
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that goes past Class 1. Things on the road go by and do not come back, so you cannot sort them into piles. You invent a way to count each kind, and you learn to tie your marks in bundles of five.
challenges.problem: For five minutes, count the autos, two-wheelers, cars and buses that pass your window or gate. At the end you must be able to say how many of each kind passed, and which kind passed the most.
constraints: You cannot stop anything or ask it to come back.
You must count four kinds at the same time.
At the end, someone else must be able to read your paper and get the same numbers.
materials: a window, balcony or gate from which you can see a road (or a lane where people walk by)
a clock or a phone timer
four small cups and a handful of beans, if you want to try counting with beans
general: Draw a table with one row for each kind. Draw one mark for each one that passes.
Draw a small picture at the start of each row, so that you do not need to read words while you watch.
Work in a pair. One person watches and calls out the kind. The other makes the marks.
creative: Tie the marks in bundles of five. Draw four marks, then draw the fifth one across them. Then you can count 5, 10, 15.
Drop one bean in a cup for each one that passes, one cup for each kind. Count the beans at the end.
Use a string for each kind and tie a knot each time one passes.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way and try it for five minutes. Then give your paper to someone at home. If they cannot read the numbers from it, change your way and try again.

flow.do: 1. Go to the window or gate together. 2. Ask your child to count the autos, two-wheelers, cars and buses for 2 minutes, in any way. 3. Do not help. 4. Ask how many of each passed.
flow.say: For two minutes, count the autos, two-wheelers, cars and buses. Use any way you like.
flow.kid: Watch the road for 2 minutes. Count each kind. Use any way you like.

good: I mixed up the autos and the cars.

flow.parent: Stay with your child near any window, balcony or gate. Most children try to hold four numbers in their head and lose them. That is the point of this step.

chart.title: What you need to find out

flow.context: This is the first step of the challenge Count What Will Not Stay Still. You try to count four kinds of vehicles on the road for two minutes.

flow.do: 1. Ask what would make the counting easier. 2. Listen to your child's ideas. 3. Read the usual ways and the creative ways aloud, if your child wants ideas. 4. Your child draws their sheet.
flow.say: What could we use so that you do not have to remember four numbers?
flow.kid: How can the paper remember for you? Think of a way. Draw your sheet.

ask.q: Why is a picture at the start of each row useful?
good: I can find the row fast.
I do not have to read.
I can keep my eyes on the road.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the challenge Count What Will Not Stay Still, where you count vehicles on the road. Here you design a sheet for counting.

flow.do: 1. Show how to tie marks in fives: four marks, and the fifth across them. 2. Your child practises with 8 marks. 3. Start a timer for 5 minutes. 4. Your child marks every vehicle that passes.
flow.say: Four marks, and the fifth goes across. That is a bundle of five. Now watch for five minutes.
flow.kid: Draw four marks. Draw the fifth across them. That is five. Now watch and mark.
flow.parent: Bundles of five are usually taught in Class 2, so plain marks are fine too. On a busy road, count only for 2 minutes, or count only autos and buses.

check.q: A row has 2 bundles of five marks and 3 loose marks. How many is that?
check.why: 13. Two bundles are 5 and 5, which is 10. Three more make 11, 12, 13. Picking 5 means counting each bundle as one mark. Picking 23 reads the 2 and the 3 as a number.

flow.context: This is step 3 of the challenge Count What Will Not Stay Still, where you count vehicles on the road. Here you learn bundles of five and count for five minutes.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts the marks in each row and writes the numbers. 2. Ask which kind passed the most and the fewest. 3. Give the paper to someone else to read.
flow.say: Count each row. Which kind passed the most? Can Paatti read your paper and get the same numbers?
flow.kid: Count each row. Which kind passed the most? Ask someone to read your paper.

ask.q: If you counted again tomorrow at the same time, would you get the same numbers?

flow.context: This is the last step of the challenge Count What Will Not Stay Still, where you count vehicles on the road. Here you read your marks and test your sheet on someone else.

items.p: How many circles are in this row? ____
items.why: Touch each circle once. There are 4 circles. The 3 squares are not counted.

items.p: Which group has the most?
items.why: Spoons. 6 is more than 4 and more than 5. The row of spoons is also the longest.

items.p: Which group has the fewest?
items.why: Dosas. 2 is less than 3 and less than 5. The row of dosas is the shortest.

items.p: You sort 10 buttons into two groups. Now there are still 10 buttons in all.
items.why: True. Sorting only moves the buttons. None was added and none was taken away.

items.p: Sort each thing: do we eat it or wear it?
items.why: Idli, banana and dosa are food. A chappal, a shirt and a cap are worn. The rule here is what we do with the thing.

items.p: Count the marks: | | | | | |   There are ____ marks.
items.why: Touch each mark once and count. There are 6 marks. Each mark stands for one thing.

items.p: Match each thing to its group.
items.why: A spoon is for eating, a crayon is for drawing, a chappal is for the feet and a comb is for the hair. Each thing is sorted by what it is used for.

items.p: These shapes were sorted into two groups. What was the rule?
items.why: By colour. Every shape in the first group is red, and every shape in the second group is blue. Each group has mixed shapes, so the rule was not shape.

items.p: How many more spoons than cups? ____
items.why: Match one spoon to one cup. Three spoons have a cup. Two spoons stick out. So there are 2 more spoons.

items.p: Put the groups in order. Start with the fewest.
items.why: 2 is the fewest, then 5, then 8. So cups come first, then lids, then spoons.

items.p: Draw 3 bananas and 5 mangoes. Draw a ring around the group that has more.
items.a: Three bananas, five mangoes, and a ring around the mangoes.
items.why: A strong drawing has exactly 3 and 5. The ring goes around the mangoes, because 5 is more than 3.

items.p: Draw one mark for each person who lives in your home. Write how many.
items.a: One mark for each person, and the number of marks.
items.why: A strong answer has the same number of marks as people at home. Say each name as you touch each mark to check.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. In the Heap Test, what rule did you make up for your own sort?
items.a: Any clear rule, such as big and small, or things that roll and things that do not.
items.why: A strong answer names one thing to look at, and the rule works for every thing in the heap.

items.p: Look at group 1 and group 2. What rule made these groups?

chart.title: Two groups

items.why: By shape. The first group is all circles and the second is all squares. Each group has mixed colours, so the rule was not colour.

items.p: Sort these by colour in your head. How many red ones? ____
items.why: Look only at the colour. There are 4 red shapes: two circles, a square and a triangle.

items.p: Sort these by shape in your head. How many triangles? ____
items.why: Look only at the shape. There are 3 triangles. Their colours do not matter for this rule.

items.p: The same toys can be sorted in more than one way.
items.why: True. You can sort toys by colour, by size or by kind. Each rule gives different groups.

items.p: The group that takes up the most room always has the most things.
items.why: False. Three big brinjals take up more room than six small lemons. Count, or match one to one, to find which has more.

items.p: How many things are there in all?
items.why: 12. Count on from 5: four more makes 9, and three more makes 12.

items.p: Match each row of marks to its number.
items.why: Count the marks in each row. One mark stands for one thing.

items.p: Sort each animal: where do they live?
items.why: A fish, a whale and an octopus live in water. A cow, a goat and a hen live on land. The rule here is the place where the animal lives.

items.p: 12 clips are sorted by colour. Then they are mixed and sorted by size. How many clips in all now?
items.why: 12. The clips were only moved. The groups changed, but no clip was added or taken away.

items.p: Put the rows of marks in order. Start with the fewest marks.
items.why: The rows have 2, 4 and 6 marks. 2 is the fewest and 6 is the most.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Name one thing at home that could go in two groups. Say both groups.
items.a: For example: a red spoon can go with the spoons or with the red things.
items.why: A strong answer names one thing and two different rules. The thing fits one group under each rule.

items.p: Draw 6 shapes. Use 2 colours. Then draw a ring around each colour group.
items.a: Six shapes in two colours, with one ring around each colour.
items.why: A strong drawing has every shape inside one ring, and each ring holds only one colour.

items.p: A red spoon is in a heap of mixed things. Which group should it go in?

views.says: With the spoons. A spoon is a spoon.
With the red things. Its colour is red.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says what the other child has right.
items.why: Both are right, for different rules. If the rule is kind, it goes with the spoons. If the rule is colour, it goes with the red things. The sorter must say the rule first.

items.p: Bananas and lemons are yellow. How many yellow fruits are there? ____
items.why: Put the bananas and lemons together. 4 and 3 make 7 yellow fruits.

items.p: 7 fruits are yellow and 2 are red. Which colour group is bigger?
items.why: Yellow. 7 is more than 2. Sorted by kind, bananas were the biggest group with 4. Sorted by colour, yellow is the biggest with 7.

items.p: A heap has 10 things. 6 are red. The rest are blue. How many are blue? ____
items.why: The red and blue groups together make 10. 6 and 4 make 10, so 4 are blue.

items.p: A heap of 7 things can have 5 red things and 5 round things.
items.why: True. Some things can be both red and round. If 3 things are red and round, then 5 are red, 5 are round, and there are still only 7 things.

items.p: Marks are tied in fives. How many marks are there?
items.why: 13. Two full fives make 10. Count on three more: 11, 12, 13.

items.p: Which one does not fit this group: idli, dosa, vada, chappal?
items.why: The chappal. Idli, dosa and vada are all food. A chappal is not food.

items.p: Sort each thing by what it is made of.
items.why: The tumbler and the plate are steel. The spoon and the ruler are wood. The bangle and the jar are glass. This rule gives three groups.

items.p: 15 things are sorted into three groups. Two groups have 6 and 5. How many are in the third group? ____
items.why: 6 and 5 make 11. Count on from 11 to 15: 12, 13, 14, 15. That is 4 more, so the third group has 4.

items.p: Put the colour groups in order. Start with the most.
items.why: 7 is the most, then 5, then 3. So red comes first, then blue, then yellow.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A shop keeps all its red things on one shelf. Is that a good way to sort a shop?
items.a: No. A shopper looks for a kind of thing, such as pens, and not for a colour. Red shirts, red pens and red apples would all be mixed together.
items.why: A strong answer says what shoppers want to find. Sorting by colour is a real sort, but it does not answer the question 'Where are the pens?'

items.p: Draw 8 marks tied in fives: one bundle of five, and the loose ones.
items.a: Four marks with a fifth across them, then three loose marks.
items.why: A strong drawing has one bundle of five and 3 loose marks. 5 and 3 make 8.

items.p: Is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable?

views.says: A vegetable. It is not sweet, and it goes in sambar and rasam.
A fruit. It grows from the flower and holds the seeds.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says what the other person has right.
items.why: Both are right, by different rules. Sorted by how we cook and eat them, tomatoes are vegetables. Sorted by the part of the plant, tomatoes are fruits, because they hold the seeds.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Think of a rule that puts you and a crow in the same group.
items.a: For example: things that are alive, things with two legs, or things that eat rice.
items.why: A strong answer names one way in which you and a crow are alike. There are many right answers.

quiz.p: What does it mean to sort things?
opts: Put things that are alike together
Put things in one long line
quiz.why: To sort is to put things that are alike together. Counting comes after sorting. A long line is not sorting unless like is put with like.

quiz.p: Look at the two groups. What was the sorting rule?
quiz.why: Colour. One group is all yellow and the other is all blue. Each group has mixed shapes, so the rule was not shape.

quiz.p: Clips, crayons and lids were sorted and counted. Which group has the most?
quiz.why: Crayons. 7 is more than 4 and more than 5. The row of crayons is the longest.

quiz.p: How many more bananas than mangoes? ____
quiz.why: Match one banana to one mango. Four bananas have a mango. Three bananas are left over. So there are 3 more bananas.

quiz.p: Autos, bikes and buses went past. Which group has the fewest?
quiz.why: Buses. 2 is less than 6 and less than 8. The row of buses is the shortest.

quiz.p: Red and blue circles and squares are sorted by colour. What is another way to sort them?
quiz.why: By shape: circles in one group and squares in the other. The same things can be sorted by more than one rule.

quiz.p: Sort these by shape. How many groups do you get?
quiz.why: 3 groups: circles, squares and triangles. The colours do not matter when the rule is shape.

quiz.p: Sorting a heap into groups changes how many things there are in all.
quiz.why: False. Sorting only moves things. If nothing is added or taken away, the number in all stays the same.

quiz.p: Groups of 5, 4 and 3 are pushed back into one heap. How many things in all?
quiz.why: 12. Count on from 5: four more makes 9, and three more makes 12.

quiz.p: Count the marks: | | | | | | | |   There are ____ marks.
quiz.why: Touch each mark once and count. There are 8 marks.

quiz.p: Four autos go by. You make one mark for each. How many marks do you draw?
quiz.why: 4 marks. One auto gets one mark. Picking 1 means making a single mark for the whole group.

quiz.p: Sorted by kind, clips are the biggest group. Sorted by colour, red is the biggest. What changed?
quiz.why: The rule changed. The things are the same and the number in all is the same. A new rule makes new groups.

quiz.p: There is only one right way to sort a heap of things.
quiz.why: False. A heap can be sorted by kind, colour, size and more. The best rule depends on what you want to find out.

applications: A vegetable seller sorts her vegetables into heaps, so that you can find the tomatoes at once.
A librarian sorts books by what they are about, so that a reader can find all the animal books together.
An ironing shop counts each family's clothes piece by piece, because the price is for each piece.
A cricket scorer makes a mark for every ball, then counts the marks to tell the runs in each over.
Families sort waste into wet and dry, so that each kind can be used again.
A doctor counts how many children had fever this week and how many had coughs, to see what is going around.
At election time, the votes are sorted by who they are for, and each pile is counted.
A bird watcher makes one mark for each bird of each kind, to find out which birds live in a place.

open_questions.q: Are some groups made by nature, or do people make all the groups?
open_questions.why_open: Thinkers have argued about this for more than two thousand years. Even for living beings, scientists do not agree on one way to say where a kind begins and ends.

open_questions.q: How do ants sort their young without anyone in charge?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have ideas, such as each ant following a simple habit. Nobody has shown for certain how the rings are made.

open_questions.q: What was the person who cut 29 marks into the Border Cave bone counting?
open_questions.why_open: The bone is about 42,000 years old and broken at one end. People have guessed days or moons, but there is no way to check.

open_questions.q: Do other animals sort the world into the same groups as we do?
open_questions.why_open: A squirrel can keep kinds of nuts apart, and a bee can tell flowers apart. But nobody knows what their groups are like for them.

ask_kids: At dinner: how could we sort the things on this table? Can you think of two ways?
On a walk: which are there more of on this road, autos or cars? How could we find out?
While putting toys away: what is your rule for where each toy goes?
At the market: why do you think the seller keeps the onions apart from the tomatoes?
Looking at family photos: in what ways are you and your cousin alike? In what ways are you different?
At bedtime: you are in many groups. Can you name three groups you belong to?

jokes.a: It could not find its pair!

jokes.j: What did the spoon say to the heap of forks?
jokes.a: I think I am in the wrong group.
The cook called it a vegetable and the scientist called it a fruit.

jokes.j: Why did the crayon sit with the apples?
jokes.a: It was red, and the rule was colour!

jokes.j: What is the laziest way to sort your toys?
jokes.a: Make one group and call it 'toys'.

jokes.j: Why did the button feel important?
jokes.a: It got a mark all to itself.

Why did the banana join the lemons?
How does a pencil count autos?
