maths.problem: You sorted a heap by kind and got 6 clips, 5 crayons and 4 lids. How many things are there in all?
maths.explain: Start with the 6 clips. Count on 5 for the crayons: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. Count on 4 for the lids: 12, 13, 14, 15. So there are 15 things in all.
maths.context: In the Heap Test you sorted one heap into groups and then counted them all together. This problem uses the same idea.
maths.why_maths: Adding the groups gives the number in all, so you can check that nothing was lost while sorting.

maths.problem: After the wash, Amma's pile has 7 clothes and Kavin's pile has 4 clothes. How many more clothes does Amma have?
maths.explain: Match one of Amma's clothes to one of Kavin's. Four of Amma's have a partner. Three do not. So Amma has 3 more.
maths.context: In Sort the Washing you sorted the dry clothes by person and counted each pile. This problem compares two piles.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two groups tells you how many more one has, which a single count cannot tell you.

maths.problem: A heap of 12 things is sorted by colour. There are 5 red things and 4 blue things. The rest are green. How many are green?
maths.explain: Red and blue together are 5 and 4, which is 9. The heap has 12. Count on from 9 to 12: 10, 11, 12. That is 3 more. So 3 things are green.
maths.context: In the Heap Test the groups always added up to the whole heap. This problem uses that to find a group nobody has counted.
maths.why_maths: Because sorting never changes the number in all, you can work out a missing group without counting it.

chart.title: 12 things in all. The green ones are not shown.

maths.problem: A fruit bowl has 4 bananas, 3 lemons and 2 apples. Sorted by kind, bananas are the biggest group. Now sort by colour: yellow and red. Which group is the biggest, and how many does it have?
maths.explain: Bananas and lemons are both yellow. 4 and 3 make 7 yellow fruits. The apples are red, and there are 2. So yellow is the biggest group. The rule changed, and so did the biggest group.
maths.context: In the Heap Test, a new sorting rule gave a new biggest group. This problem asks you to work out a new sort in your head.
maths.why_maths: Working out the new groups from the old ones shows why 'which is the most?' depends on the rule.

maths.problem: In a game of Roll and Mark, the row for 2 has 5 marks, the row for 4 has 3 marks and the row for 6 has 1 mark. The other rows are empty. How many times was the dice rolled?
maths.explain: Every roll made one mark. So count all the marks. 5 and 3 make 8, and 1 more makes 9. The dice was rolled 9 times.
maths.context: In the game Roll and Mark you drew one mark for every roll of the dice. This problem reads a finished sheet.
maths.why_maths: One mark stands for one roll, so adding the marks tells you something nobody counted during the game.

roots.context: We sorted heaps of things and counted the groups. Now let us think about where the groups come from.

deep_truth.truth: In the Heap Test, you sorted 15 things by kind and found the biggest group. Then you sorted the same things by colour, and a different group was the biggest. Nothing was added and nothing was taken away. So a heap has no biggest group until someone picks a rule.
deep_truth.habit: We ask 'Which is the most?' as if the answer were sitting in the heap. But the heap only answers after we choose how to sort it.
deep_truth.evidence: Your table from the Heap Test. It shows three rules, three different sets of groups and three different biggest groups, and 15 things in all every time.

three.who_am_i: You are in many groups at once. You are a child, a grandchild, a dosa eater and a person who lives on your street. No one group is all of you.
three.what_is_life: Other living beings sort too. Some ants keep their eggs in the middle of the nest and their biggest young around the outside.
three.what_is_this_world: The world does not come in labelled boxes. People make the boxes, and people can make them in a different way.

roots.thread: Before you sorted, there was one heap. Your rule made it into three groups. A new rule made it into different groups. Push them together and it is one heap again. The many groups and the one heap are the same things.

teachings.teaching: A father named Uddalaka tells his son: know one lump of clay, and you know everything made of clay. A pot and a cup have different names, but both are clay.
teachings.link: Sort by kind, and the pot and the cup go in two groups. Sort by what they are made of, and they go in one.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha tells of a king who had some blind men touch an elephant. One touched the ear, one the leg, one the tail. Each said the elephant was a different kind of thing, and they quarrelled.
teachings.link: Each sort is like one touch. It tells you something true about the heap, but not everything.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet, says: whatever a thing is, and whatever kind it seems to be, wisdom is to see what it truly is.
teachings.link: A group name such as 'red things' tells you one fact about a thing. The thing is always more than its group.

science.text: Ants of the kind called Temnothorax keep their young sorted by size, in rings, with the eggs in the middle (Franks and Sendova-Franks, 1992). So sorting is not only a human habit.
Are some groups made by nature, or do people make them all? Thinkers and scientists still argue about this.

other_view.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,300 years ago, and many scientists today
other_view.view: They say some groups are not our choice. A crow's chicks are crows whether or not anyone sorts them. Gold is gold and water is water. On this view, a good sorter does not make the groups. She finds the groups that are already there.

practice.title: One thing, three groups
practice.say: Pick up one small thing, such as a spoon. Look at it. Say three groups it could belong to. Now close your eyes and hold it. Feel its weight and its coolness. It is in many groups, and it is still this one spoon. Open your eyes. Was it any different when you were not naming its groups?
practice.kid: Hold one small thing. Say three groups it belongs to. Close your eyes and feel it. Is it still the same thing?

ask: If nobody sorted the heap, would it still have groups in it?
You belong to many groups. Which group feels most like you? Why?
Can two things be alike in every way? What would that mean?
Who chose the groups that you were put in, such as your class or your team?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people keep count of different kinds of things before they could write? This card tells how one scientist found out.
how_we_found_out.story: For many years, people digging at very old villages in West Asia kept finding small pieces of baked clay. The pieces were shaped like cones, balls and eggs. Nobody was sure what they were for. A scientist named Denise Schmandt-Besserat, who was born in France, studied thousands of them in museums. In the 1970s she showed that they were counters. Each shape stood for one kind of goods. An egg shape stood for a jar of oil. A cone stood for a measure of grain. Three jars of oil were shown by three egg shapes. So people sorted by shape and kept count with one piece for each thing, long before anyone could write. The oldest pieces are about 9,500 years old. She also showed that the first writing in that part of the world grew out of these counters. Most scholars now agree that writing there began with keeping count of goods. They still argue about what some of the shapes meant.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought that writing began as small pictures of things, and that counting on clay came later. Schmandt-Besserat showed that keeping count with clay pieces came first, thousands of years before writing.

science: Franks, N. R. and Sendova-Franks, A. B. (1992). Brood sorting by ants: distributing the workload over the work-surface. Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 30, 109-123. (The species was then called Leptothorax unifasciatus and is now placed in Temnothorax.)

Delgado, M. M. and Jacobs, L. F. (2017). Caching for where and what: evidence for a mnemonic strategy in a scatter-hoarder. Royal Society Open Science 4, 170958. (Fox squirrels who collected all their nuts at one spot buried each kind in its own area. Squirrels who collected nuts at several spots did not.)

Schmandt-Besserat, D. (1992). Before Writing. University of Texas Press. Also her page 'Tokens and Writing: the Cognitive Development', sites.utexas.edu/dsb: tokens from about 7500 BC, a cone for a measure of grain, an ovoid for a jar of oil, three ovoids for three jars. Later studies question whether tokens were always used one for one.
Lebombo bone: a baboon fibula with 29 notches from Border Cave, dated to about 42,000 to 43,000 years ago (d'Errico and others, 2012 and 2018). The bone is broken, and what was counted is unknown.
Annie Jump Cannon and the Harvard classification of stars (O, B, A, F, G, K, M): most sources say she classified about 350,000 stars. The Henry Draper Catalogue was published from 1918 to 1924.
Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.4 (the lump of clay). Udana 6.4, Tittha Sutta (the blind men and the elephant). Thirukkural 355 (seeing the true nature of a thing, whatever its kind).

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Heap Test works with any 15 small things in 3 kinds and 3 or more colours. The number in all comes out the same after every sort unless something rolls away, so sort on paper or plates. The example numbers in the charts (6, 5 and 4, then 7, 5 and 3) were checked to add up to 15. Guess My Rule was played in the head with a colour rule, a shape rule and a size rule: a round takes 2 to 6 cards. Roll and Mark ends within 25 rolls. Step minutes add up to each activity's minutes. Ant Watch needs ants and about 10 minutes of waiting, and it is not in the core path. The stretch challenge needs a grown-up at the window or gate.
